text:
The history of mechanical timekeeping is in large part a history of escapements. An escapement is the part of a clock that releases the driving power in small, regular increments, and it is the component that turns a falling weight or an unwinding spring into a countable rhythm. Without one, a weight simply falls and a spring simply unwinds; with one, the same energy is metered out in discrete steps that can be counted, displayed, and compared against the motion of the sun.

The earliest European mechanical clocks, which appeared in the late thirteenth century, used a verge escapement paired with a foliot, a horizontal bar carrying two adjustable weights. The foliot had no natural period of its own. Its rate depended on the driving force, on the friction in the train, and on where the weights happened to sit along the bar, which meant that two clocks built to the same drawing would keep different time, and that a single clock would change its rate as its lubricant thickened or its rope frayed. Monastic communities, which were the main customers, cared less about this than one might expect. What they needed was a device that would ring a bell at roughly the right hour, and a sundial was available on clear days to correct the drift.

The decisive change came in the middle of the seventeenth century, when Christiaan Huygens applied the pendulum to clockwork. Galileo had observed that a swinging weight keeps a period that depends mainly on its length and hardly at all on the width of its swing, at least for small swings. A pendulum therefore has a natural period that the clock can be built around, rather than a rate that the clock imposes upon it. The escapement's job changed accordingly: instead of setting the rate, it now had only to give the pendulum a small push on each swing to replace the energy lost to air resistance and pivot friction, and to count the swings. Accuracy improved by roughly two orders of magnitude within a few decades, from a quarter of an hour a day to well under a minute.

This distinction, between a timekeeper whose rate is set by the driving mechanism and one whose rate is set by an independent oscillator, turned out to matter far beyond clocks. It is the same distinction that separates a circuit clocked by a resistor and capacitor from one clocked by a quartz crystal, and it explains why the second is now defined by an atomic transition rather than by the rotation of the earth. An oscillator that does not care what is driving it can be made better in isolation, tested against another of its kind, and improved without redesigning everything attached to it.

Marine navigation supplied the hardest version of the problem. Longitude at sea can be found by comparing local noon against the time at a reference meridian, but that requires carrying the reference time aboard a moving, rolling, temperature-varying ship, where a pendulum is useless. John Harrison spent much of his life on the question, and his answer was not a better pendulum but a different oscillator entirely: a balance wheel controlled by a spring, arranged so that changes in temperature would compensate rather than accumulate. His fourth timepiece, tested on a voyage to Jamaica, lost only a few seconds over more than two months at sea.

What is worth noticing about this sequence is how often the improvement came from removing a dependency rather than from refining a part. The foliot depended on the driving force; the pendulum did not. The pendulum depended on gravity and on standing still; the balance wheel did not. Each step traded a component that had to be made well for an arrangement in which making it well mattered less. Engineers in other fields have rediscovered the same pattern many times, usually after a long period of trying to polish the component instead.
